dēspectus , ūs, m. despicio.
I. A looking down upon; hence, a view or prospect from an elevated place (repeatedly in Caes.; elsewh. rare; “not in Cic.): erat ex oppido Alesia despectus in campum,” Caes. B. G. 7, 79, 3 : “in mare,” id. ib. 3, 14
fin.: “sub terras,” Lucr. 4, 417 : “qua longe pelago despectus aperto,” Stat. Th. 5, 351 .—In plur., concr., points of view, heights: “cum ex omnibus partibus altissimas rupes despectusque haberet (oppidum),” Caes. B. G. 2, 29, 3 .—
II. Transf. (only dat.), a spectacle, an object of contempt: “despectui me habet,” Vulg. Gen. 16, 5 ; id. 2 Esdr. 4, 4.—
B. A despising, contempt: “ludibrio et despectui esse oppositum,” Auct. Her. 4, 39, 51 .
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
